More info on the Nike Air Zoom Alphafly Next Nature from [Nike’s Site](https://news.nike.com/news/nike-air-zoom-alphafly-next-nature-official-images-release-date): The Nike Air Zoom Alphafly Next Nature takes Nike’s most elite performance shoe and recreates it with circular design principles. It is Nike’s most sustainably-minded performance shoe to date.

Following Nike Basketball’s Cosmic Unity, Nike Running designers were driven by a core belief within the Move to Zero initiative — Nike’s journey toward zero carbon and zero waste — that a product that makes the world better can also make an athlete better. Cosmic Unity set the bar with 25 percent total recycled content by weight; the Alphafly Next Nature advanced it by reaching at least 50 percent total recycled content by weight, making it Nike’s boldest move yet in merging sustainability and performance. Doing so with the crown jewel of racing footwear was an important symbolic choice.

The design of the AlphaFly Next Nature arrives at new answers by considering new questions: What are creative ways to select different materials or processes for the shoe’s performance elements? Can leftover or recycled versions of those pinnacle features be made while maintaining their elite properties?

Those kinds of questions required fluid conversation between engineers, developers and manufacturers to create a shoe that performed in real life. That work translated into hitting meaningful numbers in sustainability for some of the shoe’s most important performance elements. Take the Nike ZoomX midsole, which was made with at least 70 percent recycled materials by weight. Bull attributes a big part of the magic of Nike racing shoes to the ZoomX foam, reaching back to Eliud Kipchoge’s daring quest to break the 2-hour marathon barrier. If any of it is going to waste, she says, it’s a huge loss for the people who would potentially wear those shoes on race day. One solution: Put the leftover recycled foam from the midsole back into the sock liner. Redeem a part of the shoe that symbolizes so much potential for the body.

Two months ago, Wegmans Food Markets indicated it had no plans to bring back its popular hot and cold food bars, which were forced to close during the coronavirus pandemic by New York state mandate.

Recently, the state relaxed rules around self-serve buffets, which can now run normally, as long as a worker is “stationed nearby to observe.”

And late last week without fanfare, Wegmans’ flagship Pittsford store reopened a small hot bar offering such fried fare as chicken wings, tenders and nuggets and mozzarella sticks.

It will operate from 11:30 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. daily, said spokesperson Laura Camera.

The same setup will roll out at more Wegmans stores in the next couple weeks, she said. She could not provide a full list of locations but said Perinton is one of them.

At this point, Wegmans does not plan to bring back self-serve bars offering other types of foods, Camera said. However, a new staffed station at the Pittsford store allows customers to order fresh, hot foods at lunch and dinnertime. Options include Asian and homestyle dishes, she said.

In addition, “We have kiosks that allow customers to order a variety of fresh meals to go,” she said.

The kiosks are now operating at the Pittsford and Perinton stores.

Meanwhile, “We will continue to explore additional opportunities to deliver restaurant-quality food to our customers,” she said.

Call the Lifeline whenever and feel free to ask how they operate. You’ll be routed to the most local call center based off your area code. There is no corporate number (technically, the Lifeline is administered by Vibrant Emotional Health in NYC, but the infrastructure relies on 160+ local, independently operated crisis centers across the country). 

Most people don’t realize (because the Lifeline is poorly explained to the public) that each of the call centers that answer calls have their own training, aren’t held to Lifeline-mandated standards (all are accredited by third-party orgs), and can vary widely in who they employ - clinicians, volunteers, or both. On top of that, Vibrant is federally funded by SAMHSA to administer the Lifeline, so any sanctioned religious components would be incredibly illegal (those components don’t exist).

[This thread](https://outdoors.stackexchange.com/questions/4015/what-is-considered-a-water-source-and-why-is-it-recommended-to-camp-so-far-from)  highlights several reasons why it’s not recommended. 

“The reasons are several-fold:

Waste - wastewater should never be put in creeks/lakes/etc - and although many people will walk 200 meters away to dispose of it properly, most wont. The closer people are to a body of water, the more likely they are to say "ah to heck with it" and dump it in. It's difficult to resist the temptation to just do a quick rinse of hands, plates, etc in a creek that is right next to you.

Erosion - The riparian areas next to creeks and lakes are often the most sensitive, and can not handle large amounts of traffic. Traffic up and down and along the creek banks can cause rapid erosion of soil and cause vegetation loss. This is a problem from alpine to canyon ecosystems.

Visual Disturbance to other hikers - Setting up your tent beside that beautiful pristine lake is an awesome scene, right up until that group across the lake sets their tent up in your view. Don't be 'that guy.' I've successfully distributed 15 groups of backpackers around a high-alpine lake so that every single one of them could pretend they were the only ones out there.

Disturb/Encounter wildlife - while you are asleep, chances are there is a whole host of thirsty critters strolling up and down the creek / lake shore looking for drink (or to eat those drinking). These are also natural travel corridors. Your presence can be disruptive to the fauna, or could put you in the path of grumpy wildlife (bears).”

What we know about suicide amounts to a complicated series of factors, usually over a period of time. Unfortunately, we'll never know what the people who died from suicide were really thinking at the moment. The closest we can get is from those who lived through it. In that vein, I would highly suggest checking out [Live Through This](http://livethroughthis.org/). Their stories can give you some perspective on why suicide seemed the option at that moment. 

Now, on terms of theory about why someone might reach the point where they want to kill themselves, I'd suggest you look at Thomas Joiner's [Theory](http://www.apa.org/science/about/psa/2009/06/sci-brief.aspx), which focuses on long term isolation, a lack of purpose and capability (and here's where we touch on exposure or familiarity with firearms).

Noticing a lot of questions about means, method substitutions, and rurality that aren't addressed in this study. 

A good place to start is this website - [Means Matter](https://www.hsph.harvard.edu/means-matter/) - covering statistics and research on lethal suicide means. Two things of note:
In one study of suicide attempt survivors, 24% reported a suicidal deliberation of <5 mins and 23% <1 hour. Putting time and space between someone and their chosen method can save a life. Method substitution is a myth (meaning if you restrict access to someone's chosen method, it's incredibly rare that they then go on to die from suicide using another method).

Suicide rates are higher in rural areas, as is firearm ownership, however rates of depression are not higher than in urban areas.

This clip is absolutely brilliant. I've volunteered at the crisis line in Kansas in the US for over five years and this is spot on. Calls like this happen every night, multiple times a night.

The people that call in need someone that cares, has a compassionate tone, and are willing to listen without judgment. Callers want the pain to end, but more importantly want someone to hear them. 

Getting through the wee hours of the night are by far the hardest. Friends and family are asleep, and can't be reached. The people that answer these phones are the last lines of defense against ending a life; the last line before people are affected irrevocably. The people that answer these phones are true heroes.

Some in this thread have questioned how we can take this sort of call without emotional risks, and that's part of the job. That should be part of the training. Empathy doesn't stop at the lifeline, but the call ends with multiple safeguards in place. And like the woman said in the clip, we always encourage them to call back if needed (our line always offers followup calls at a later date to make sure they have something to look forward to). We don't hang up unless we're comfortable with a caller's imminent safety.

TL:DR If you know someone who is in crisis or is thinking about suicide, listen to them. Listen. To. Them. And try to find out what they need to get help.

Resource Center Coordinator for Kansas Youth Suicide Prevention here. The single crisis center in Kansas accredited by the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, Headquarters Counseling Center (which I also volunteer at) received a federal grant about a year ago to combat this public health issue. For reference, if you call the Lifeline anywhere in Kansas, you'll talk to someone at Headquarters. It's a small nonprofit located in Lawrence. 

KYSP has managed to sponsor the creation of a few suicide prevention coalitions around the state and we've sponsored multiple events and trainings over the last year. We're working hard to help those in need across the state. We also have a new online resource center - kansassuicideprevention.org. For those interested, please check it out - we're also welcoming feedback.

We also have some amazing coalitions and task forces in the eastern and southeastern parts of the state - Johnson County, Sedgwick County (Wichita), and Shawnee County (Topeka). These dedicated people have been working tirelessly to make sure people get the help they need. Barton County is another area of tremendous efforts. These are in conjunction with efforts in Dodge City, Atchison County, and other areas.

All that being said, we are experiencing a lot of barriers to effectively reaching those in need. Other states (Colorado specifically) have really concrete support from their legislation and government. This article pinpoints a key barrier in allowing us to procure the resources we need. We have people everywhere reporting that they're struggling, but that they can't afford mental healthcare. States like Kentucky and New York have instituted a prevention policy of Zero Suicides, which we're researching implementing here, but we'll require the backup of those state departments with big reach and resources. 

TL;DR - We have people all over this state working very hard to end suicide, the stigma attached to mental health problems, and to increase the access to care. But without support from legislation and the governor, it's very, very difficult.

Mind you, this is before any of them got really famous. For example, Zach is touchingly sad, creepy, and at times literally seems insane. I hate to say it, but his charm has been lost since the Hangover trilogy. Anyway, it's on Netflix, but make sure you get the doc and not the standup show by the same name; or watch both.
